The patient presents with a new-onset, severe bilateral temporal headache (10/10, dull ache), but critical elements needed to narrow the differential are *absent or indeterminate*: onset timing (thunderclap vs. gradual), associated neurological signs/symptoms (e.g., neck stiffness, photophobia, focal deficits), and results of definitive diagnostic tests (non-contrast CT head, LP, MRI). Crucially, *no positive findings* support any specific diagnosis yet — BP is normal (argues against hypertensive emergency), labs show no inflammation (ESR/CRP normal), no systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, jaw claudication), no hematologic abnormalities, and no reported visual disturbance or scalp tenderness. While temporal location raises suspicion for giant cell arteritis (GCA), the patient lacks age-related risk (not stated — but GCA is rare <50), no jaw claudication, no scalp tenderness, no visual symptoms, and normal inflammatory markers — all strongly arguing *against* GCA. Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) remains possible but cannot be confirmed or excluded without non-contrast CT or LP; however, absence of thunderclap onset (indeterminate), no nausea/vomiting, no photophobia/meningismus (unreported but not confirmed on exam), and normal vitals make SAH *less likely pending testing*, though still urgent to rule out. More immediately, given the lack of corroborating features for secondary causes *and* the bilateral temporal localization, the leading *primary* headache consideration consistent with available data is **tension-type headache (TTH)** — specifically, *probable episodic tension-type headache*, since it is bilateral, pressing/tightening (described as “dull ache”), non-pulsating, mild-to-moderate (though here rated 10/10 — severity discordance warrants caution), and without nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia (not reported, but also not affirmed absent).
